1.explanation: At tick 5 the Mixer is working on loaf 3 and the Oven on loaf 1; the Packer holds no loaf, so it is idle.

2.explanation: Loaf 1 is already packed, but loaves 2-4 still need packing: loaf 2 is in the Oven and loaves 3-4 are waiting for it. Work the Packer will need exists upstream but has not reached it yet.
2.howToFind: Type 'at 8' (the Packer's line says why it is idle); 'explain starved' for the definition.

3.explanation: All 4 loaves were mixed by tick 8, so no loaf will ever need the Mixer again. That is not starvation.

4.explanation: Over ticks 0-19 the Oven worked 16 of 19 ticks, the Mixer 8 and the Packer 4.
4.howToFind: Type 'util' (the whole run is the default period); 'explain utilization'.

5.official: Idle 15 ticks, starved for all 15 of them.
5.explanation: The Packer needs 1 tick per loaf, but loaves only leave the Oven every 4 ticks. Between loaves it is starved: the Oven sets its pace. Its low utilization says it waits for upstream work, not that it is unnecessary.

6.explanation: The Oven bakes loaf 3 (ticks 6-10) and loaf 4 (ticks 8-12) at the same time.

7.explanation: Its slots are starved at the start (6 slot-ticks while the first loaves are mixed) and have no work left at the end (4 slot-ticks after the last loaf went in).
7.howToFind: Type 'util', then 'machine Oven' for where the idle slot-ticks are.

8.explanation: In the middle of the run both slots are always baking. The whole-run figure is lower only because of the start and the end.

9.explanation: Packer 2 finished loaf 2 at tick 12; its next loaf (4) is still in the Oven until tick 14.

10.explanation: Without Packer 2 the order finishes at tick 37 instead of 30.

11.explanation: Without Oven 2 the order still finishes at tick 37. Packing sets the pace in version B, so the second oven only shortens the wait in front of the Packer.

12.official: The Oven and the Packer, tied at 84% (32 of 38 ticks) each.

13.official: No; no; only adding an oven and a packer together (38 -> 24).
13.explanation: The Oven and the Packer limit the order together: with only one of them doubled, the other still sets the same pace. This is where the bottleneck concept begins.
